g.text: DistanceFunc — chosen once, never branched on
bool — stored vectors are unit length (Cosine)
int — tombstoned slots; the compaction signal
uint64 — mutation count, re-checked at Compact's swap
atomic.Uint64 — Calibrate's ef factor, not serialized
[]int — a neighbor list copied out under its lock
*nodeLocks — non-nil only in a batch worker
bool — tombstone: dead as an answer, alive as a route
atomic.Bool — edges still being built in a batch; others step around it

div.h3: How a node picks its top layer
div.p: Exponentially decaying: most nodes stop at layer 0, a few reach high. That is what makes the top sparse and the descent cheap. The RNG is seeded, so the serial path replaying the same inserts in the same order rebuilds an identical graph — which is what makes Compact testable by equality. InsertBatch links on several workers and is not deterministic: WithInsertWorkers(1) + WithSeed for that.

g.text: A slot outlives its vector — delete AND update

div.p: Keeping the M nearest produces edges that all point into the same cluster, and searches strand in local minima.
Instead, drop candidate c when it already sits closer to an already-chosen neighbor s than to the node itself — you could reach c by hopping through s, so that edge buys nothing:

alpha = 1.0 — classic HNSW heuristic, and the default. alpha > 1.0 rejects less: more near candidates survive and, arriving nearest-first, take the slots long-range edges needed. At 62.5K × 512 in 1,024 tight clusters, alpha 1.2 never passed recall 0.954 at any ef; 1.0 reached 0.95 at ef=10. Do not "restore" the DiskANN value.
Rejected candidates are backfilled if the list comes up short — a node with too few edges is a dead end during search.

div.h3: Delete(id) — a tombstone, never a removal
div.p: delete(ids, id) · deleted = true · numDeleted++ · re-elect the entry if this slot was the entry.

The slot keeps its index and every edge. It has to: slots are addressed by index, so removing one would shift every index above it and invalidate every neighbor list in the graph. And a node is a bridge — cut it out and a neighborhood nobody deleted becomes unreachable.
div.h3: Insert(id, v) on a live id — an upsert
div.p: Same three steps, then a brand-new slot is built for v with a fresh random level. The old slot is never edited in place: its inbound edges were chosen for the old vector, and pruning makes edges asymmetric, so finding them all is an O(N·M) scan of the whole graph.
Unchanged vector → early return, no slot spent. That is the WAL-replay path.
div.h3: What a tombstone costs until compaction
div.p: cands (the frontier) admits it — a dead node still bridges. results never does — a dead node is not an answer. So the search widens instead of returning fewer than k hits: 1.2× at 25% dead, 1.6× at 50%, 2.5× at 75%. pruneConnections demotes tombstones so they cannot evict a fresh live edge.
div.h3: Compact() — the only thing that gives the memory back
div.p: Builds a new graph over the live vectors and swaps it in whole. It cannot renumber the live one: neighbor lists are slot indices, so removing a slot invalidates every list in the graph at once.

Out comes exactly the graph you would have built if the dead vectors had never existed — fresh RNG from the same seed, live vectors in slot order — so it is testable by equality rather than by sampling recall.

Searches and writes keep running. The replacement is built holding no lock on the live graph — ids and stored vectors never change once placed. place / tombstone record each id they touch in dirty; catch-up rounds set those ids in the replacement to their current state, then the swap takes the write lock. DB.Compact holds writeMu only for the last catch-up and the swap.

The build tracks survivors: 2.61 s at 25% dead against 0.79 s at 75%, per 5k × 128. Compacting early costs more and reclaims less, so the index never self-triggers — callers poll Stats().DeadRatio(); ~0.5 is the threshold.
vector — dim × 4 bytes neighbors — up to 2M 8-byte ints on L0 + M per upper layer; at M=16: up to 256 B on L0, plus slice headers (the codec writes them as uint32: 662 B/vector on disk at 128 dims)
3 KiB/vector → 1M vectors ≈ 3 GiB, graph overhead is minor
512 B/vector → the neighbor lists are the same order as the data
Know which regime you are in — it decides whether quantization or graph compaction is the optimization that matters.
